Skin Effect Disadvantages in AC Systems

Skin effect disadvantages all come from one cause: AC current crowds into a thin outer layer, so the useful cross section of the conductor shrinks. A smaller effective area means higher AC resistance, more I²R heating and wasted copper or aluminium at the centre. The higher the frequency, the worse each problem becomes.

DisadvantageWhy it happensWhere it shows up
Higher AC resistanceCurrent flows only in about one skin depth near the surfaceLarge cables, busbars, transformer windings
Extra I²R heatingSame current through a smaller areaCables and transformers carrying harmonic currents
Wasted conductor materialThe centre of a thick conductor carries almost no currentCopper conductors much thicker than twice the skin depth
Need for deratingHarmonics have higher frequency and a thinner skinNeutrals and transformers feeding drives and rectifiers
Poor AC performance of steelHigh permeability gives a very thin skinSteel conductors and magnetic parts
Loss at high frequencySkin depth falls below half a millimetre at tens of kHzSMPS transformers, inductors, RF circuits

In copper the skin depth is about 9.3 mm at 50 Hz but only about 0.066 mm at 1 MHz, so the same wire that works well on a power line becomes lossy in a switching converter. Engineers limit these disadvantages with hollow or tubular conductors, stranded and Litz wire, and by applying AC correction factors when sizing large busbars and cables.
